analysis.one_liner: Requires a plan to rebuild depleted New England cod and haddock stocks by restricting fishing, with buybacks and retraining for fishermen.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the groundfish rebuilding bill in September 1992, but the full House never voted on it and the Senate never acted before the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced an amendment to the Northeast fishery management plan to eliminate overfishing of cod within seven years and haddock within ten, with immediate closures of spawning areas and a moratorium on new fishing permits [S3]. To cushion the fleet, it created a program to buy out fishing vessels, allowed fishermen to temporarily switch to underutilized species like mackerel and skates, and offered retraining and income support to fishermen put out of work [S4]. It also directed negotiations with Canada over shared fish stocks and set up a voluntary on-board data collection program [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal fishing communities and seafood consumers benefit over the long run from restored cod and haddock stocks. Fishermen facing restrictions would get vessel buyback payments, transition assistance, job retraining, and income support, and the bill would relax federal fishing vessel loan guarantees only toward plans consistent with conservation [S3] [S4].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the New England Fishery Management Council to submit a plan amendment eliminating overfishing of cod stocks within seven years and haddock stocks within ten, and lets the Commerce Secretary write the amendment itself if the Council does not act [S3]
Requires immediate closure, within five days, of areas where groundfish are spawning or where undersized fish concentrate [S3]
Creates a vessel purchase (buyback) program to reduce the number of boats and fishing effort in the groundfish fishery [S4]
Authorizes job training, adjustment assistance, and needs-related income payments for fishermen unemployed because of the fishing restrictions, with $10 million authorized for the first year [S4]

Sets up a program of joint ventures and grants to develop fisheries for underutilized species such as mackerel, dogfish, and skates, conditioned on fishermen temporarily surrendering their groundfish permits [S4]
Directs the State Department to negotiate a fishery agreement with Canada covering transboundary groundfish stocks in the northwest Atlantic [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Owners of groundfish fishing vessels would bear new catch restrictions, permit penalties, and a new diesel fuel tax on their boats during the moratorium, which funds the buyback and enforcement programs. Taxpayers would fund the fisherman retraining grants [S4].

drawbacks.text: The fishing restrictions would idle boats and cut crews' income in the short term, which is why the bill pairs them with buybacks and transition aid; the diesel fuel tax would also raise operating costs on the same fleet during the moratorium [S4]

The amended version reported by the committee declares that the Council and the Commerce Secretary cannot be held to account for any past failure to prepare a rebuilding program for cod, yellowtail flounder, and haddock, a legal shield for the agencies responsible for the depletion [S3]

A moratorium on new permits while existing permits are renewed could concentrate the fishery among current permit holders, and the vessel buyback's price-setting advisory panel includes brokers and insurers with a stake in vessel values [S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: rebuilding collapsed fish stocks requires cutting fishing now, and that costs boat owners and crews money today for a healthier fishery later. The bill softens the blow with buybacks, tax relief on idle vessels, and retraining money, which makes it more politically palatable but also more expensive for taxpayers. The provision exempting the Council and the Commerce Department from liability for their past failure to rebuild the stocks is the biggest design flaw, since it removes accountability from the very offices the bill was meant to pressure.

outcome.mechanism: The Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee reported the bill in amended form on September 22, 1992, but the House never scheduled a vote and the Senate took no action before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerry Studds, chairman of the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee, introduced the bill on July 16, 1991, and it was referred to three House committees [S6]

The Fisheries Subcommittee held hearings, including field hearings in Boston in September 1991 and Galilee, Rhode Island in January 1992, and forwarded an amended bill to the full committee in May 1992 [S6]
The full committee ordered the bill reported on July 1, 1992, and formally reported it amended on September 22, 1992, as House Report 102-885 [S6]
The reported version changed the goal from doubling the spawning biomass of groundfish within five years to eliminating overfishing of cod within seven years and haddock within ten [S2] [S3]
No further House action occurred and the Senate never considered the bill; the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of the New England groundfish fleet were better off, since no new catch restrictions, permit moratorium, or diesel fuel tax took effect through this bill. The responsible fishery managers also avoided the binding deadlines and accountability the bill would have imposed, while the depleted stocks got no mandatory rebuilding plan from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of the unrestricted groundfish fleet

for.name: Rep. Gerry Studds
for.role: Chairman, House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, held hearings including field hearings in New England fishing ports, and steered it through his committee to a September 1992 report.

for.name: House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill, amended it, ordered it reported on July 1, 1992, and reported it amended on September 22, 1992.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote in the months after the committee reported it.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it received no Senate hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was written and advanced by a Democratic committee chairman with one Republican cosponsor, and it never reached a floor vote, so there is no record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would restrict the fleet's fishing through catch cuts, spawning closures, permit penalties, and a diesel fuel tax, but it pays vessel owners for boats through a buyback, allows withdrawals from capital construction funds for idle-vessel costs, and offers retraining and income support to displaced crews. The industry's interest in continued unrestricted fishing runs against restoring the public fish stock, though the bill pays it to shrink.

The bill authorizes grants and joint ventures to help processors develop markets for underutilized species like mackerel, dogfish, and skates, giving them new supply while reducing pressure on groundfish.

industries.industry: Recreational fishing interests (Sport Fish Restoration Account)
industries.note: The vessel buyback and enforcement programs would draw on the Sport Fish Restoration Account, funded largely by angler excise taxes, though the bill caps such spending at 20 percent of the account in a year and only to the extent of new diesel-tax deposits from fishing vessels.

industries.industry: Marine lenders and ship mortgage guarantee program
industries.note: Federal loan guarantees could no longer go to vessels or facilities inconsistent with the groundfish plan, restricting financing for fleet expansion, while guarantees for underutilized-species fisheries would be encouraged.
